headline: Under AGI by 2036, factory operators plan other work before 2039 robots while some worry that a distant date invites delay.

whatTheyDo.text: 142 of 202 plan other job options: one worker watches a hospital jobs board for maintenance openings.
135 plan retraining: a young operator would start a college maths refresher before seeking an electrical apprenticeship.
131 save more: one worker puts away 50 to 80 a month as pay rises.
64 wait for more information: one worker delays choosing a course while watching how the decade develops.
50 continue present work: one operator stays on the night press and works on the scrap rate.

whatTheySay: **A decade opens paths:** younger workers describe building a trade, technician career or business before the robots arrive.
**Present wages still pay the bills:** midlife workers discuss mortgages and children even after the longer runway.
**A retirement date needs figures:** older workers ask whether documented income can cover housing, food and repairs.
whatTheyThink: **More time can become an excuse:** some privately expect to postpone training for years.
**Savings buy choices, not lifetime income:** middle-aged workers see reserves as a buffer while future vacancies remain uncertain.
**Later-life work is conditional:** older workers need verified retirement figures before counting on an exit.
howTheyFeel: **Unease is common:** 100 of 202 are uneasy, with time to plan but no guaranteed job after robots.
**Income risk still drives anxiety:** 84 are anxious and three alarmed, often with thin reserves or wages needed after 2039.
**Some feel calm:** 15 are calm and describe concrete paths into trades, technical work or businesses.

differences.text: On the 1–5 worry scale, thin-cushion profiles average 2.875 (n=72), versus 1.968 for strong cushions (n=63).
Resistant profiles average 2.588 (n=68), versus 2.119 for adaptive profiles (n=67), on the 1–5 worry scale.
Late-stage profiles average 2.575 (n=40), midlife 2.432 (n=81) and early-stage 2.210 (n=81) on the 1–5 worry scale.

quotes.name: Yusuf Rahman
quotes.text: Ten years is long enough to drift, and I've seen guys at my plant promise a course for five years running. I'd set myself deadlines and tell my girlfriend.

quotes.name: Colin Schmidt
quotes.text: My dad sat in the kitchen for a year after the steelworks shut.

quotes.name: Sara Patel
quotes.text: A date on the tile factory calendar will not pay our food bill.

least.name: Early career builders
least.story: All 15 least worried are early-stage and adaptive; their private answers describe trades, technician careers or businesses before the robot date.

most.name: Wages still needed
most.story: Of the 87 most worried, 62 have thin cushions; many mention mortgages, rent or uncertain future work despite the extra years.

thoughts.text: A distant robot date could make me delay preparing.
The 2039 robot date still shapes my work or family timeline.
A decade gives me time to build another work route before robots.
Current wages or savings give me room to plan.
Retirement before the robots depends on real income covering bills.
I need viable paid work even after the longer warning.
